sections.title: Modal verbs that do not change
sections.content:
When there is a modal verb in the original statement, suggestion, etc., it sometimes changes when we report what was said or thought. However, some modal verbs do not change: could, would, should, might, needn't, ought to, used to, could have, should have, etc.
• 'I could meet you at the airport.' → He said that he could meet us at the airport.
• 'We might drop in if we have time.' → They said they might drop in if they have time.

sections.title: will, can, may
sections.content:
The modal verbs will, can, may usually change to would, could, might when reported:
• 'She may have already left.' → He thought she might have already left.
If the situation we are reporting still exists or is still in the future, and the verb in the reporting clause has a present tense, we use will, can, may in the reported clause:
• 'Careful! You'll fall through the ice!' → I warn him he will fall through the ice.
If the situation we are reporting still exists or is still in the future, and the verb in the reporting clause has a past tense, we can use either would or will, can or could, or may or might in the reported clause:
• 'The problem can be solved.' → They said the problem can / could be solved.

sections.title: shall
sections.content:
Shall changes to would when talking about the future:
• 'I shall (I'll) call you on Monday.' → She told me she would call me on Monday.
Shall changes to should in offers, requests for advice, etc.:
• 'Where shall I put this box?' → He asked where he should put the box.

sections.title: must and mustn't
sections.content:
Must (= necessity) changes to must or had to:
• 'You must be home by 9 o'clock.' → She said I must / had to be home by 9 o'clock.
Must (= conclude) and mustn't do not change:
• 'I didn't hear the phone. I must be going deaf.' → Alex thought he must be going deaf.
• 'You mustn't tell my brother.' → He warned me that I mustn't tell his brother.

sections.title: Adding a modal verb in the report
sections.content:
We sometimes use a modal verb in a reported sentence when there is no modal verb in the original:
• 'You're not allowed to smoke here.' → She told me that I mustn't smoke there.
• 'My advice is to look for a new job now.' → She said that I should look for a new job now.

exercises.question: The doctor says that he ___ see you in 20 minutes.
exercises.hint: If the reporting verb is in the present tense ('says') and refers to the future, use 'will'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: will
If the reporting verb is in the present tense ('says') and refers to the future, use 'will'.

exercises.sentence: She said that she can help us move house at the weekend.
exercises.correction: She said that she could help us move house at the weekend.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: she could help us
In reported speech, modal verbs shift back: can → could, will → would, may → might, must → had to, shall → should/would. 'Can' becomes 'could' in reported past tense. Note: 'could', 'would', 'might', 'should', and 'ought to' do not change.

exercises.question: In her letter, Elizabeth revealed that she ___ be getting married soon.
exercises.hint: If the reporting verb is in the past tense but the event is still in the future, both 'may' and 'might' can be used.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: both
If the reporting verb is in the past tense but the event is still in the future, both 'may' and 'might' can be used.

exercises.sentence: He told me that I must to leave the building immediately.
exercises.correction: He told me that I had to leave the building immediately.
exercises.hint: In reported past speech, 'must' (obligation) shifts to 'had to'. Also: no 'to' after modal verbs.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I had to leave
Two issues: (1) 'Must' expressing obligation shifts to 'had to' in reported speech. (2) All modals are followed by a bare infinitive — no 'to'. 'Must to leave' is always wrong. Note: 'must' expressing logical deduction can stay as 'must' in reported speech: 'He said it must be true.'

exercises.question: 'I won't be late.' → She promised ___ late and she kept her word.
exercises.hint: Use a that-clause with 'wouldn't' because the reporting verb is past ('promised') and referring to a past future.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: that she wouldn't be
Use a that-clause with 'wouldn't' because the reporting verb is past ('promised') and referring to a past future. 'Would' and 'used to' both express past habits, but 'would' cannot be used for past states — only repeated actions.

exercises.question: She told me she ___ (might / consider) the offer if the salary was right.
exercises.hint: 'Might' does not change in reported speech.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: might consider
'Might', 'could', 'would', 'should', and 'ought to' do not change in reported speech — they are already past or hypothetical forms. Only 'can', 'will', 'may', 'must', and 'shall' shift back: can→could, will→would, may→might, must→had to, shall→should/would.

exercises.question: 'I must be getting old.' → She said that she ___ getting old.
exercises.hint: When 'must' expresses a conclusion, it doesn't change to 'had to' in reported speech.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: must be
When 'must' expresses a conclusion, it doesn't change to 'had to' in reported speech.

exercises.question: 'If you want to travel with us, that's fine.' → She said that ___
options: I had to travel with them.
exercises.hint: 'Can' (meaning permission or ability in the original intent) changes to 'could' in reported speech.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: I could travel with them.
'Can' (meaning permission or ability in the original intent) changes to 'could' in reported speech. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.
